title: Circle the faster reaction
asks: Two reactions differ in one thing. Circle the one that goes faster.

know.h: Rate laws. {{SN2}}: rate = k[substrate][nucleophile]. {{SN1}}: rate = k[substrate] only. {{E2}}: rate = k[substrate][base]. A change in the nucleophile (its strength or its concentration) changes the rate of {{SN2}} but not of {{SN1}}.
What each mechanism needs. {{SN2}}: low sterics, good nucleophile, good leaving group, polar aprotic solvent. {{SN1}}: stable carbocation, poor nucleophile, good leaving group, polar protic solvent.
Substrate in {{SN2}} (relative rates): allyl 1.3; methyl 1; ethyl 0.033; isobutyl 0.003; isopropyl 0.00083; tert-butyl 0; vinyl 0. Steric hindrance slows the approaching nucleophile.
Substrate in {{SN1}}: tertiary > secondary; primary and methyl do not react by {{SN1}}. Allyl does (the carbocation is stabilized by resonance); vinyl does not.

Vinyl and aryl halides (leaving group on an {{sp2}} carbon of a C=C or a benzene ring) do not undergo {{SN2}} or {{SN1}}. A better leaving group does not rescue them. Allyl and benzyl halides, with the leaving group on the {{sp3}} carbon next door, react well.

Nucleophile strength (relative {{SN2}} rates): {{HC≡C-}} 126,000; {{HS-}} 126,000; {{I-}} 80,000; {{HO-}} 16,000; {{N3-}} 8,000; {{NH3}} 8,000; {{Cl-}} 1,000; {{CH3CO2-}} 630; {{CH3OH}} 1; {{H2O}} 1. An anion beats its conjugate acid; a bulky nucleophile such as tert-butoxide is slow.

Leaving group: the weaker the base, the better it leaves. I > Br > Cl >> F among the halides (HI {{pKa}} -10, HBr -9, HCl -8, HF 4). Tosylate, OTs, is a good leaving group. {{HO-}} and {{RO-}} are strong bases and poor leaving groups: an alcohol with {{HS-}} gives no reaction.
The leaving group leaves in the rate-determining step of both {{SN2}} and {{SN1}}, so a better leaving group speeds up both.
Solvent types. Polar protic (hydrogen bond donors): {{H2O}}, {{CH3OH}}, {{CH3CH2OH}}, acetic acid. Polar aprotic: DMSO, DMF, acetone, acetonitrile.
Solvent and {{SN2}}: with an anionic nucleophile, a polar aprotic solvent is faster, because a protic solvent hydrogen bonds to the nucleophile and holds it back.
Solvent and {{SN1}}: increasing the polarity of the solvent increases the rate, because the transition state of the ionization is stabilized more than the neutral starting compound.

Solvent polarity and charge. If charge is created on the way to the transition state (neutral amine and alkyl iodide), a more polar solvent is faster. If charge is destroyed ({{HO-}} and a sulfonium cation), a less polar solvent is faster.
Skill: compare the two reactions item by item (substrate carbon, leaving group, nucleophile, solvent, concentrations) and name the single difference before thinking about rates.

Skill: decide the mechanism from the substrate and conditions (methyl or primary with a good nucleophile: {{SN2}}; tertiary with no strong base in a protic solvent: {{SN1}}; tertiary with a strong base: {{E2}}).

method: Compare the two reactions piece by piece and name the one thing that differs: nucleophile, leaving group, substrate carbon, solvent or concentration.
Find the carbon that carries the leaving group. If it is an {{sp2}} carbon (vinyl or aryl), that reaction does not go, and the other one wins.
Decide the mechanism from the substrate class and the conditions: {{SN2}}, {{SN1}} or {{E2}}.
Ask whether the thing that differs appears in that mechanism's rate law or in its rate-determining step.
Apply the matching rule or number: nucleophile table, leaving group order, Figure 7.3, carbocation stability, or solvent type.
Circle the faster reaction and say in one line what differs and why it matters for this mechanism.

pitfalls.h: Ranking substrates before reading the conditions: tertiary is the slowest in {{SN2}} and the fastest in {{SN1}}.
Choosing the better leaving group when it sits on a vinyl or aryl carbon. No {{SN2}} and no {{SN1}} happen there.
Mixing up allyl (leaving group next to the double bond: fast) and vinyl (leaving group on the double bond: no reaction).
Saying that polar aprotic solvents are always faster. That is true for {{SN2}} with an anionic nucleophile; {{SN1}} is faster in polar protic solvents.
Saying that concentration of the nucleophile or base never matters for a tertiary halide. With a strong base the reaction is {{E2}}, and the base is in the rate law.
Treating all primary halides as equal: branching on the next carbon (isobutyl, 0.003) slows {{SN2}} about tenfold.
